One photo, twelve components

Every effect on this page is built from a single lake photo. Each one comes with the sentence that asks for it.

Pick a component, copy its sentence, attach your own photo and paste both into Claude or ChatGPT. That is the whole method.

Nothing here loads a library. It is one file of HTML, CSS and a little JavaScript, so each effect is small enough for an assistant to write in one reply.

Pan and zoom

A still photo that moves slowly reads as film. Use it to open a page or to hold a quote.

Ask for it like this

Fill the frame with my photo and zoom in very slowly toward the island, like a documentary shot. Loop it back out.
Effort
Easy. One sentence.
Made here with
One CSS animation
Grow into
GSAP or Motion, for timed sequences of shots
Seen in

Scrolling photo tour

The photo stays put while the text scrolls. Each paragraph moves the camera to the part it talks about.

1 of 7

  1. Start wide

    One frame, 2016 by 1512 pixels, taken from the shore under full cloud.

  2. The sky does most of the work

    Cloud fills the top 57% of the picture. That much even tone is why text sits on it so easily.

  3. The far shore

    A band of evergreens crosses the frame just past halfway down. It is the darkest strip in the photo.

  4. The island

    To the right of the trunk a small wooded island stands taller than the shoreline behind it.

  5. The detail you would miss

    A single bare shrub stands in open water. Zooming is how a page says: look here.

  6. The tree

    The trunk runs the full height of the frame and splits it into a wide part and a narrow part.

  7. The reeds

    Dry cattails and fallen leaves fill the bottom third. They are the only warm colours in the picture.

Ask for it like this

Pin my photo while I scroll. I will give you seven short paragraphs. For each one, zoom the photo to the part it describes.
Effort
Moderate. You say where to look; expect one round of nudging the zooms.
Made here with
Sticky positioning and an IntersectionObserver
Grow into
Scrollama, the step-trigger library used in newsrooms
Seen in
The Pudding, and the New York Times feature Snow Fall

Self-drawing line art

A sketch that draws itself as you scroll, then gives way to the real photo. The treeline, island and trunk were traced from the photo's own pixels.

Keep scrolling. Far shore first, then the tree, then the reeds, then the photo.

Ask for it like this

Trace the main shapes in my photo as a simple line drawing. Draw the lines as I scroll, far things first, then fade the real photo in underneath.
Effort
Harder. The assistant has to analyse the photo. Ask for a looser sketch if the first one is off.
Made here with
SVG paths and stroke-dashoffset, tied to scroll
Grow into
GSAP DrawSVG or Anime.js; Lottie or Rive for animation drawn by a designer
Seen in
Explainer intros and Codrops demos

Chart from the photo

A chart is a component too. These numbers are measured from the photo, so the chart and the picture tell the same story.

Ask for it like this

Measure how bright my photo is from top to bottom and chart it as a line with a soft fill. Put a strip of the real colours under the axis. Label only the highest and lowest points, and let me touch the chart to read the rest.
Effort
Moderate. The chart is easy; ask the assistant to show how it measured.
Made here with
Hand-written SVG, sized to your screen
Grow into
Observable Plot for quick charts, D3 for custom ones, ECharts for dashboards
Seen in
The Pudding's data stories

Swipe gallery

Cards in a row that snap into place one at a time. On a phone it is the most natural way to browse a set.

The island

Evergreens on a low rise, right of the trunk.

The shrub

Alone in open water, easy to miss at full size.

The bark

The trunk and a few bare branches against cloud.

The cattails

Dry stalks and seed heads along the near shore.

The far shore

A thin dark line of trees between sky and water.

The cloud

Soft bands of grey and blue, most of the picture.

Free tools to grow into

  • GSAPThe standard for scroll and timeline animation. Free with every plugin, under its own no-charge licence.
  • MotionAnimation for React, Vue and plain JavaScript. MIT licence.
  • Anime.jsSmall and friendly, strong on SVG. MIT licence.
  • ScrollamaStep triggers for scrollytelling. MIT licence.
  • LenisSmooth scrolling that other effects sit on top of.
  • Built into browsersScroll-driven animations and view transitions now work without any library.
  • Observable PlotA chart in a few lines. ISC licence.
  • D3Total control for custom charts. ISC licence.
  • Apache EChartsA large catalogue of interactive charts. Apache 2.0 licence.
  • shadcn/uiAccessible components you copy into your project.
  • Magic UIAnimated components for landing pages. MIT licence.
  • Aceternity UIDramatic, dark, cinematic components.
  • React BitsAnimated text, backgrounds and cards with open source.
  • Three.js, Lottie and RiveFor 3D scenes and for animation drawn by a designer.

Behind this page

The keynote voice sells a vision by removing everything else. Inspired by Steve Jobs's product launches. The company and every figure here are invented for the demo.

How it is built

  1. The world as it is, as one painful number
  2. The consequence, said quietly
  3. A question that opens the door
  4. The answer in three words
  5. One image and the new number
  6. Before and after, side by side
  7. One more thing
  8. A closing line short enough to repeat

Design rules

  • One idea per screen. If it needs two sentences, it is two screens.
  • Black background, one typeface, white and grey only
  • Numbers are the pictures. Make them enormous.
  • The rule of three: three words, three steps, three benefits
  • One photograph, used once, full screen
  • Each screen snaps into place and its words arrive in order

Turn my notes into a keynote-style page: one idea per screen, huge type, almost no words.

The storyteller voice. Inspired by Donald Miller's story framework. Use it when the reader should see themselves in the problem and act.

A full example follows. How it is built, and the sentence that asks for it

The hook

At 6:40 on a Tuesday evening, walking the dog along the water, Priya finally sent the message she had been putting off for a year.

A character who wants something

She wanted a kitchen her family could actually eat in. Not a showroom. A table that fit four people and a counter where the kettle did not have to be moved to make toast.

It had taken her a year to ask. Asking meant admitting the old kitchen had won.

She typed four sentences, pressed send, and put the phone back in her pocket.

The problem

Then nothing happened.

  • On the surfaceThree companies had her message. By Wednesday night, none had answered.
  • UnderneathShe began to feel foolish for asking. Maybe the job was too small. Maybe she had filled in the form wrong.
  • Why it is wrongNobody should have to chase a company to give it their money.
A guide appears

We know, because we were the ones who went quiet.

For years our own replies took a day or more. Not because we did not care. Because the person who could answer was on a ladder in someone else's kitchen.

So we changed one thing. Now a reply is drafted the moment a message arrives, and a person reads it, fixes it and sends it. In a 90-day trial, 81 of every 100 people heard from us within the hour.

The plan

Three steps, and only the first is yours.

  1. You write to us once. Four sentences is plenty.
  2. A real person answers within the hour, in working hours.
  3. That first reply offers you two dates for a visit.
The call to action

What is at stake
If nothing changesAnother year of moving the kettle. Another form sent into silence. The quiet conclusion that it was never going to happen.
If you write tonightAn answer before bed. A date in the diary. Someone in your kitchen this week with a tape measure and a pencil.
The ending

Priya's phone buzzed before she reached the end of the path. On Thursday someone stood in her kitchen with a tape measure.

The reply was not the work. It was the proof that the work would be done.

Behind this page

The storyteller voice makes the customer the hero and the company the guide. Inspired by Donald Miller's story framework. Priya, the company and the figures are invented for the demo.

How it is built

  1. A hook: one moment, one person, a time on the clock
  2. A character who wants something specific
  3. A problem at three depths: on the surface, underneath, and why it is wrong
  4. A guide who shows empathy first, then proof
  5. A plan in three steps
  6. One call to action
  7. The stakes: failure beside success
  8. An ending that returns to the opening, and a line that lingers

Design rules

  • Photography leads. Slow push-ins and a window that drifts, like a nature film.
  • One reading column, large serif type, generous space
  • The story beat is named above each part, small, in the accent colour
  • One pull quote per screen at most
  • The company does not appear until the fourth beat
  • Colours come from the photograph: dusk, sand and ember

Short ask: one sentence

Tell this as a story on one page, with my customer as the hero and us as the guide. Use my photo large.

Full ask: you name the voice, look and parts

Write a one-page story from my notes. Hero: my customer. Open on one moment with a time and a place. Give the problem at three depths, then introduce us as the guide with empathy before proof, a three-step plan, one button, the stakes side by side, and an ending that returns to the opening. Dark warm page, large serif type, my photo with a slow push-in. Take the colours from the photo.

Use the artifact-studio skill. Recipe: landing page. Voice: storyteller. Look: take the palette from my attached photo. Content: the attached customer interview notes. Invent nothing about the customer; where a story beat has no material, ask me one question.

The teacher voice. Inspired by David Malan's lectures. Use it when the reader should understand how something works.

A full example follows. How it is built, and the sentence that asks for it

Today's question

How do you answer everyone within the hour, without hiring anyone?

Think of it as

The host at a busy restaurant.

The host does not cook your meal. The host looks up, says "we see you, your table is nearly ready", and tells the kitchen you are here. You stop wondering whether to leave.

A first reply does the same job. It is not the quote. It is the looking up.

A real example

One enquiry, minute by minute

  1. 6:40A message arrives through the website form.
  2. 6:41A draft reply is ready. It thanks her by name, repeats what she asked for and offers two visit dates.
  3. 6:55The office manager reads it, changes one date and presses send.
  4. 6:56The customer has an answer. Sixteen minutes, start to finish.
In pseudocode

First, the simple version

when an enquiry arrives:  if the office is closed:    send "got it, reply by 9"  draft a reply from our template  if the draft contains a guess:    mark the guess  show the draft to a person  if the person approves:    send it

Press Step to walk through it one line at a time.

Check yourself

Three questions before you go

Why does a person still press send?

Because a draft can be wrong, and a wrong promise costs more than a slow one. The machine does the typing. The person does the deciding.

What should the first reply never include?

A price. The host does not quote the bill at the door. The first reply confirms, sets a time and stops.

What happens at 2 in the morning?

Lines 2 and 3. An instant note says a person will reply by 9. The draft waits for that person.

So

The first reply is the looking up, not the meal. Draft it by machine. Send it by hand.

The teacher voice makes a hard idea feel obvious by starting somewhere familiar. Inspired by David Malan's lectures. The company and the timings are invented for the demo.

How it is built

  1. One question, stated plainly
  2. An everyday analogy in very large type
  3. One concrete example with real times
  4. The same idea as pseudocode, stepped through line by line
  5. A harder case, handled by lines already on the board
  6. Questions to check understanding
  7. A one-sentence recap that reuses the analogy

Design rules

  • Black and white, with one highlight colour that means "look here"
  • The analogy gets the biggest type on the page
  • Complexity rises one step at a time, never two
  • Code is set in a monospace face with numbered lines
  • Every section is tagged with what kind of thing it is
  • The reader does something: steps through, then answers

The pitch voice. Inspired by Don Draper's carousel pitch in Mad Men. Use it when the reader should feel something first and remember it.

A full example follows. How it is built, and the sentence that asks for it

My father kept a hardware shop. There was a bell over the door. When it rang, he looked up. Every time.

He did not always have what you came for. But you knew you had been seen.

Somewhere along the way, we swapped the bell for a form. A form does not look up.

26 hours.That is how long someone stands at our door now.

You know that silence. You have stood in it yourself.

So this is not a faster reply. It is not software. It is not a process.

It is the bell.The First Hour. Every enquiry, answered by a person.

We are going to look up again.

1 of 6

What they will remember

In the trial, 81 of every 100 people heard from us within the hour. They will not remember the number.

They will remember that on an ordinary evening, they rang the bell, and somebody looked up.

Behind this page

The pitch voice sells a feeling and lets the product arrive last. Inspired by Don Draper's carousel pitch in Mad Men. The father, the shop and the figures are invented for the demo.

How it is built

  1. A personal memory, in the first person
  2. The feeling inside that memory
  3. What was lost, in one image
  4. The single hard fact
  5. What this is not, three times
  6. What it is: the feeling, renamed as the product
  7. A quiet close that returns to the memory

Design rules

  • A dark room and one lit rectangle, like a slide projector
  • One slide at a time, advanced by hand
  • Photographs look remembered: faded, warm, soft at the edges
  • Never more than three short sentences under a slide
  • The product name appears once, on the last slide
  • No bullet points, no charts, no feature list

Short ask: one sentence

Pitch this as a feeling, not a feature. First person, a handful of slides, and the product named only at the end.

Full ask: you name the voice, look and parts

Build a six-slide pitch from my notes that I advance by hand. Dark background with one lit slide at a time. Open with a personal memory in the first person, name the feeling, show what was lost, give one hard fact, say three things this is not, then name the product as the feeling. Make my photos look like faded film. End with a short close below the slides.

The practical instructor voice. Inspired by a best guess at Bradley Ross's teaching style. Use it when the reader should do the thing today.

A full example follows. How it is built, and the sentence that asks for it

Answer in the first hour.

The core idea: a machine drafts the reply, a person sends it. You get speed without giving up judgement.

Think of it as a sous-chef.The chopping is done before you walk in. You still taste the dish and you still plate it. Nobody gets served something you have not seen.

Why bother

26 htypical wait before the change
38 mintypical wait after 90 days
+13more site visits a month

Example figures, invented for this demo.

Do it today

Five steps, about an hour. Tick them off as you go.

0 of 5 done

Three levels

Stop at the level that is enough for you.

LevelWhat you doWhat it takes
BeginnerPaste each enquiry into a chat with your rulesAn hour, no accounts to connect
AdvancedA saved project with your voice file, price list and visit calendarAn afternoon
ExpertYour inbox is connected. Drafts appear on their own and you approve them.A connected mailbox and a weekly check

Where people go wrong

  • Letting it send by itself. A person approves every reply. No exceptions.
  • Putting a price in the first reply. Confirm, offer a time, stop.
  • Skipping the test on old enquiries. Five tests find most of the problems.
Your next step: open your sent mail and find three replies you are proud of.

The practical instructor voice gets someone doing the thing within the hour. A best guess at Bradley Ross's teaching style: core concept, one analogy, steps for today. The company and figures are invented for the demo.

How it is built

  1. The core idea in one sentence

The analyst voice. Inspired by Barbara Minto's pyramid principle. Use it when the reader should be convinced by evidence.

A full example follows. How it is built, and the sentence that asks for it

First-reply trial, 90 days. Prepared for the owners.

Replying within the hour raised booked site visits by 72%. Make it the standard.

The answer

Adopt drafted first replies with human approval for all enquiries. The trial paid for itself in the first month and reduced staff time.

38 minmedian first reply, down from 26 h
31site visits a month, up from 18
2.5 hstaff time a week, down from 6 h

Example figures, invented for this demo.

Finding 1Reply time fell from 26 hours to under an hour by week 8, and stayed there

Median hours from enquiry to first reply, by week. Touch the chart to read a week.

So what: the change held after the first month, when attention usually drifts.

Finding 2Booked site visits rose every month of the trial

Before18
Month 122
Month 228
Month 331

Site visits booked per month. "Before" is the average of the three months before the trial.

So what: 13 more visits a month. At the usual one job in four, that is about three more jobs.

Finding 3Staff spent less time on replies, not more

Hours a week, before6.0
Hours a week, after2.5

Office manager's own time log, weeks 9 to 13 against the month before the trial.

So what: the gain does not depend on anyone working longer.

How we measured

  • All 214 enquiries received in the 90 days
  • Reply time taken from mailbox timestamps
  • Visits counted from the shared calendar

What this does not show

  • One company and no comparison group
  • Spring is the busy season, so some of the rise is seasonal
  • Jobs won lag visits by weeks. That number is not in yet.

Behind this page

The analyst voice gives the answer first and then earns it with evidence. Inspired by Barbara Minto's pyramid principle. The company and every figure are invented for the demo.

How it is built

  1. A title that is the conclusion, not the topic
  2. The answer in two sentences
  3. Three numbers that carry it
  4. Three findings. Each heading is a full sentence, each has one chart and a "so what".
  5. How it was measured
  6. What the evidence does not show
  7. Next steps with an owner and a date

Design rules

  • Quiet page, one data colour, grey for the comparison
  • Every chart has one job and says its unit
  • Label the values that matter and leave the rest to touch
  • Sources sit under each chart in small type
  • Limits get the same space as method
  • No decoration that is not data

Write this up as an evidence-first one-pager: the answer at the top, then three findings with a chart each.

Full ask: you name the voice, look and parts

The executive brief voice. Inspired by the board or cabinet decision memo. Use it when the reader should make a decision in three minutes.

A full example follows. How it is built, and the sentence that asks for it

Decision brief: a one-hour standard for first replies

To
The owners
From
Office manager
Date
12 May
Decision needed by
26 May
Reading time
Three minutes

Decision required

Approve option C: every enquiry receives a first reply within one working hour, drafted automatically and sent by a member of staff. Cost: about $150 a month.

Background

1.Enquiries reach us by web form, email and telephone. Before the trial our median first reply took 26 hours, and 12% of enquiries were answered within the hour.

2.From February to April we trialled drafted replies. Median reply time fell to 38 minutes, 81% of enquiries were answered within the hour, and booked site visits rose from 18 to 31 a month.

3.The trial ends on 31 May. Without a decision we return to the previous arrangement.

Options

OptionCost a yearExpected resultMain risk
A. Return to the previous arrangementNoneReplies in about a day. Visits return to about 18 a month.Lost work we never hear about
B. Hire a part-time coordinatorAbout $26,000Replies within the hour in office hoursCover for holidays and illness
C. Drafted replies, sent by staff (recommended)About $1,800As measured in the trialA wrong draft sent unread

Recommendation

4.Option C. It delivers the result of option B at about one fifteenth of the cost, and it has already been tested here for 90 days.

Risks and controls

  • A draft is sent without being read. Control: nothing sends without a named member of staff pressing send. Reviewed monthly.
  • The first reply promises too much. Control: first replies confirm and offer a visit. They never state a price.
  • The result was seasonal. Control: measure again in November and report to the owners.

Next steps if approved

5.Standard takes effect 1 June. Office manager reports reply times and visits on the first Monday of each month.

Example brief. The company, the dates and every figure are invented for this demo.

Behind this page

The executive brief voice exists to get a decision from busy people. It is the plainest voice here on purpose. It follows the convention of a board or cabinet decision memo. The company and figures are invented for the demo.

How it is built

  1. A header: to, from, date, and when the decision is needed
  2. The decision, stated before anything else
  3. Background in numbered paragraphs, facts only
  4. Options in one table, including "do nothing"
  5. The recommendation and the reason in two sentences
  6. Risks, each with its control
  7. What happens next if the answer is yes

Design rules

  • It looks like a document: one column, serif text, a paper page
  • No images and no animation. Movement would cost trust.
  • Numbered paragraphs, so people can say "see paragraph 2"
  • One table, with the recommended row shaded
  • One accent colour, used for rules and headings
  • Short enough to read in three minutes, and it says so

Serif type, one navy accent, no images, no animation.

The scrolling explainer recipe. A scrolling explainer teaches a process one stage at a time while a diagram keeps the reader's place.

A full example follows, with invented content. How it is built, and the sentence that asks for it

How a quote gets made

Five stages between your first message and a price you can trust. Scroll and the diagram keeps your place.

  1. Stage 1. You, then the office

    You tell us what you want

    A few sentences and a photo are enough. We reply within the hour to book a visit. No price yet, because nobody has seen the room.

    Takes you about five minutes.

  2. Stage 2. The estimator

    Someone comes to look

    The estimator walks the room with you and asks what annoys you about it now. That answer shapes the design more than any measurement.

    About 45 minutes at your home.

  3. Stage 3. The estimator

    Everything is measured and listed

    Walls, windows, pipes and sockets go on a drawing. Then every item the job needs goes on a list: 41 lines for a typical kitchen.

    This list is what makes the price reliable.

  4. Stage 4. The office

    Each line gets a price

    Materials come from this month's supplier prices. Labour comes from how long the same task took on our last ten jobs. Then an allowance for the unknown.

    A typical allowance is 8% of the total.

  5. Stage 5. A second person

    Someone else checks it

    A person who did not write the quote reads it against the drawing. Only then does it go to you, with three options and a date it is valid until.

    You have it within three working days of the visit.

Five stages, two people, three days. That is why the number does not change later.

hours. That is how long they waited for us.

Behind this deck

The visionary deck is for a room. It makes people feel that something has changed, and it leaves the detail for the conversation afterwards. It follows the manner of Steve Jobs's product launches: a villain, one rule, three things, one number, and a quiet last slide. The company and figures are invented.

How it is built

  1. Open on the feeling, in one sentence
  2. Name the villain as a single number
  3. Say what the villain cost
  4. State the idea as one rule
  5. Three things, three words
  6. The proof: one number, with the old one struck through
  7. What the proof bought
  8. "One more thing": the easiest possible next step

Design rules

  • Black background, white type, one grey for everything secondary
  • One idea on each slide, and never more than about ten words
  • Numbers larger than anything else on the screen
  • No bullet lists, no logo on every slide, no footer
  • No pictures unless the picture is the idea
  • The speaker carries the detail. The slide carries the beat. Each slide has a note for the speaker: tap Notes or press N

The person

Name what happened, then how it felt. The feeling is the real problem.

The guide

We have been the company that wrote back late.

Our replies took 26 hours. We changed one rule, and now they take 38 minutes.

Now we may enter, as the guide. One line of empathy, one proof.

Three steps, and the first is free.

  2. We visit, measure and listen.
  3. You get one clear price with three options.
Three steps, and make the first one cost nothing.

Start with two photos

If nothing changes

Another winter of the drawer that sticks and the light you never liked.

How it ends

Friends in the kitchen, and you not apologising for it.

    One number and what it means. Portrait takes more of the screen than a square.

  • Story 1080 by 1920

    Full screen and upright. Keep words out of the top and bottom sixth, where apps put their own buttons.

  • Carousel, slide 1 1080 by 1350

    A swipe-through post. Slide one is the hook and must stand alone.

  • Carousel, slide 2 1080 by 1350

    The middle slides carry one idea each. Number them.

  • Carousel, slide 3 1080 by 1350

    The last slide is the ask. One action only.

  • Link preview 1200 by 630

    The picture shown when your page is shared as a link. Wide, with the title large enough to read small.

Behind these formats

A post is read in about a second, on a phone, among other posts. So each format carries one idea in very large type, and the brand is a small line at the bottom. The sizes are the common ones. Platforms change their preferred sizes, so check the platform before a campaign.

How they are built

  1. Each format is one SVG drawing at its real pixel size
  2. Text is set line by line, so nothing reflows by surprise
  3. The download button writes the fonts into the file, then saves a PNG at full size
  4. The story reads its photograph from the page, so swapping the page photo swaps the story

Design rules

  • One idea per picture. If it needs two, make a carousel
  • The first carousel slide must make sense alone
  • Seven words or fewer in the headline
  • Keep words away from the edges, and out of the top and bottom sixth of a story
  • Strong contrast: most people see it at thumbnail size first
  • The last slide asks for one action

Short ask: one sentence

Make a square social post from this one sentence, in my colours.

Full ask: you name the voice, look and parts

Make three social pictures from my notes: a square post with my main claim in seven words or fewer, a portrait post with my best number and a before-and-after bar, and a link preview with the page title. Use the colours in my attached spec, very large type, and my company name small at the bottom. Give me each as a PNG at full size.

With the skill: it does the whole job

Use the artifact-studio skill. Templates: social square, portrait stat and link preview. Content: the attached notes. Invent no facts.

Page components

Twelve building blocks that need no photograph. These are the plain parts most business pages are made of. Each one comes with the sentence that asks for it. All figures are invented for the demo.

Questions and answers

Each question opens on a tap. People read only the ones they came with.

Does anything get sent without a person seeing it?

No. Every reply waits for a named member of staff to read it and press send.

What if the draft is wrong?

Edit it, or delete it and write your own. Guesses are marked so you check those first.

How long does it take to set up?

About an hour for one mailbox, using three replies you have already sent.

Behind these parts

Each file is plain SVG with its animation written in CSS inside the file. That means it plays as an image, inside a page, or pasted into a slide tool that accepts SVG. Colours come from four variables with built-in fallbacks, so a page can recolour a part by setting them.

How to use one

  1. As an image: <img src="line-draw.svg" alt="...">
  2. Inline: paste the file's contents into the page. Its styles are scoped to its own id, so parts do not clash
  3. To recolour inline, set --ink, --accent, --soft or --sand on the page
  4. To change a number, edit the text and the one value the description names
  5. Where SVG is not accepted, such as email, use the GIF copy in components/gif/

Design rules

  • The resting picture is the finished picture. Motion only brings it in
  • One movement per part, under three seconds, or a slow loop
  • No script and no outside files
  • A title and a description inside every file, for screen readers and for agents
  • Motion stops under "reduce motion"

Short ask: one sentence

Where the look comes from

Use the first of these that applies.

  1. The person's design spec or brand colours. Follow it exactly.
  2. An image they supplied. Take the palette from it with the method below.
  3. The default for the chosen voice. See the last table in this file.

Taking colours from a photo

  1. Find the five or six colours that cover most of the picture. Ask for them by share, largest first.
  2. The darkest becomes the text colour, and the background for dark bands.
  3. The lightest, or a paler step of the largest colour, becomes the page background.
  4. The most vivid colour that is not skin or sky becomes the accent. Use it sparingly.
  5. Check text against its background: 4.5 to 1 or better. Darken or lighten until it passes.
  6. Name each colour for the thing it came from (fog, pine, reed). It keeps choices honest.

A cool photo gives a calm page. A warm photo gives an emotional one. Do not fight the picture.

Clean

Field
Feels like A well-edited reference page
Layout One column, generous margins, clear headings, short sections
Type One typeface. Size and weight carry the hierarchy
Colour Neutral background, one accent colour used sparingly
Motion None, or a gentle fade on load
Avoid Decoration, gradients, more than one accent, centred body text

Cinematic

Field
Feels like A film title sequence
Layout Full-height sections, one idea per screen, large imagery or dark colour fields
Type Very large display headings, small quiet body text
Colour Dark base, one strong highlight
Motion Slow reveals as each section enters. Nothing that loops
Avoid Dense text, small images, busy navigation, anything that moves constantly

Scrollytelling

Field
Feels like A guided walk through a story or a process
Layout A visual that stays in place while short text steps scroll past it and change it
Type Short paragraphs, one per step, large enough to read while scrolling
Colour Calm base. The highlight follows the current step
Motion Tied to scrolling. The reader controls the pace
Avoid More than about seven steps, steps longer than three sentences, motion that plays on its own

Dashboard

Field
Feels like An instrument panel
Layout The few numbers that matter at the top, supporting charts below, details last
Type Tabular numbers, compact labels, units always shown
Colour Neutral. Colour only for status and for separating series
Motion None
Avoid Decorative charts, unlabeled axes, more than one question per chart

Editorial

Field
Feels like A magazine feature
Layout A narrow reading column, pull quotes, the occasional wide image
Type A serif for reading, a contrasting face for headings, comfortable line spacing
Colour Paper-like background, dark text, one accent
Motion None
Avoid Sidebars, wide text columns, anything that interrupts the read

Keynote black

Field
Feels like A product launch in a dark theatre
Layout One idea per full screen, centred. Screens snap into place
Type One sans serif, bold, very tight. Numbers larger than anything else
Colour Black, white and two greys. At most one colour, used once
Motion Words rise into place as each screen arrives
Avoid Bullet lists, small charts, any second typeface

Paper memo

Field
Feels like A printed decision paper on a desk
Layout One page-shaped column on a grey surround. A header block, numbered paragraphs, one table
Type A serif for text, a plain sans for headings and labels
Colour White paper, near-black text, one dark accent for rules and headings
Motion None
Avoid Images, icons, coloured panels, anything that moves

Field guide

Field
Feels like A workbook you write in
Layout Boxed blocks on squared paper. Numbered steps with tick boxes. Tables for comparisons
Type A condensed bold face for headings, a wide plain sans for text
Colour Two colours: a dark one for structure and a bright one that means "act"
Motion Only in response to the reader: a tick, a progress bar
Avoid Soft shadows, gradients, long paragraphs

Faded film

Field
Feels like A slide projector in a dark room
Layout One lit rectangle at a time, a few words beneath it
Type A high-contrast serif for the few large words, italic serif for captions
Colour Warm near-black, cream, and the browns of an old photograph
Motion Slides advance by hand. Captions fade up
Avoid Crisp saturated photos, sans serif type, anything that looks new

Cards

A card is a box that holds one thing: one article, one number, one person, one offer. Six kinds cover most pages. Each comes with the sentence that asks for it. All names and figures are invented.

  • One subject for each card. If you need the word "and" to describe it, make two cards.
  • The most important thing first. A reader should get the point from the top third.
  • One main action. A second action is quieter. A third belongs on the page the card leads to.
  • The same padding and the same order in every card of a row. Rows line up because the cards match.
  • No card inside a card, and a light hand with shadows. A border or a soft tint is usually enough.

Summary card

A title, one line and a way in. The plain card that leads to more detail. Use it for a list of services, articles or projects.

Kitchen design

We measure, draw three layouts and price each one.

See how it works

Fitting

One team from first day to last, with a named lead.

See a week on site

Aftercare

A visit at six weeks, and a number that is answered.

Read the promise

Layouts

A layout decides where the eye goes first and what it meets next. Six cover most pages. Pick by what the reader has to do, not by what looks new.

The reader has toUse
Read something throughSingle column
Scan a long page for the part they needHeadings down the left
Do one thingCorner to corner
Weigh two things, or see a picture beside a messageSplit screen
Browse many things of one kindCard grid
Take in several different things at a glanceBento grid

Single column

One column of text at a comfortable width, with nothing beside it. The layout for anything meant to be read from top to bottom.

  • Use it for reports, explainers, letters, anything over 300 words.
  • The rule keep lines to about 60 to 75 characters. Wider than that and readers lose their place.
  • Avoid it when the reader is comparing things. A column hides one option while showing another.

Ask for it like this

Lay this out as one reading column, about 65 characters wide, centred on wide screens. Nothing in the margins.
Effort
Easy. One sentence.
Made here with
CSS max-width in ch units
Grow into
A scrolling explainer with a picture that changes beside the column
Use it for
Reports, explainers, letters

Headings down the left

On a long page people read the first lines across, then run down the left edge looking for a heading that matters to them. This is often called the F-pattern. Give the left edge something worth finding.

  • Use it for guides, questions and answers, policies, search results.
  • The rule start every heading and every first sentence with the words that carry the meaning. "Refunds: 14 days" beats "Information about our approach to refunds".
  • Avoid it when the page has one job. Then the reader should not have to hunt.

Ask for it like this

This page will be scanned, not read. Put a plain heading on every section, start each heading with its key word, and put the answer in the first sentence under it.
Effort
Easy. Mostly a writing job.
Made here with
HTML headings in order, no script
Grow into
A contents list that follows you down the page
Use it for
Guides, questions and answers, long reports

Corner to corner

On a page with few words the eye starts top left, crosses to the top right, drops diagonally and ends bottom right. This is the Z-pattern. Put your name where the eye starts and the button where it ends.

  • Use it for landing pages, sign-up pages, a social picture, the first screen of a proposal.
  • The rule one action, placed where the eye finishes. A long page repeats the shape: picture left then right, section by section.
  • Avoid it when there is a lot to read. The eye will not zigzag through paragraphs.

Ask for it like this

Make the first screen follow the eye from corner to corner: our name top left, one small link top right, the main message low on the left and one button low on the right. One action only.
Effort
Easy. One sentence.
Made here with
CSS grid
Grow into
Sections that alternate picture and text down the page
Use it for
Landing pages, sign-up pages, first screens

Split screen

Two halves of equal weight: a message and a picture, or two choices. On a phone the halves stack, so decide which comes first.

  • Use it for a message that needs its picture, a before and after, a choice between two paths.
  • The rule the halves must be equals. If one is clearly less important, it is a sidebar, and a sidebar should be narrower.
  • Avoid it when there are three things. Three halves do not exist.

Ask for it like this

Make this a split screen: the message and one button on the left, my photo filling the right. On a phone, show the message first and the photo under it.
Effort
Easy with a photo attached
Made here with
CSS grid, two equal columns
Grow into
A before and after slider, from the photo parts
Use it for
Landing pages, case studies, a choice of two

Card grid

Rows of matching cards. Nothing is more important than anything else, which is the point: the reader browses and chooses.

  • Use it for products, services, articles, a team, anything where the items are of one kind.
  • The rule every card the same height, every picture the same shape, the same order inside each.
  • Avoid it when one item matters most. A grid cannot say so.

Ask for it like this

Show these as a card grid: three across on a wide screen, one on a phone. Every card the same height and every photo the same shape.
Effort
Easy. One sentence.
Made here with
CSS grid with auto-fit
Grow into
Filters, when there are more than nine
Use it for
Products, services, articles, team pages

Bento grid

Tiles of different sizes packed into one block, like a lunch box. One tile is clearly the largest. The rest support it.

  • Use it for a summary of several different things: a result, a quote, a number, a picture.
  • The rule one dominant tile. Keep the same padding and the same corner in every tile, or it looks like a jumble.
  • Avoid it when the items are of one kind. Then it is a card grid pretending.

Ask for it like this

Summarise this as a bento grid: one large tile for the main result, and four or five smaller tiles for a number, a quote, a photo and the next step. Same padding and corners on every tile. Stack to one column on a phone.
Effort
Medium. Decide the main tile first.
Made here with

Grow into

Use it for
Summaries, launch pages, a year in review

Colour

Most pages need fewer colours than people expect: a background, a text colour, a few quiet greys and one colour that means "act here". These five ideas are enough to choose them well.

  • Mostly quiet, a little loud. About 60 parts background, 30 parts text and structure, 10 parts accent.
  • One accent. It marks what to act on. If it is also used for decoration, it stops meaning anything.
  • Greys with a trace of your colour. Pure grey looks dead beside a brand colour. A slight tint makes them belong together.
  • Check every pair of text and background. 4.5 to 1 for ordinary text, 3 to 1 for large text, 7 to 1 if you can.
  • Never colour alone. If red means late, the word "late" is there too.

A palette from one colour

Give it the one colour you already have, as a position on the colour wheel from 0 to 359. It returns seven colours with a job each, and checks every pair of text and background. The first one shown is hue 45.

Your headline goes here

Secondary text sits quietly beside it.

A highlight inside a panel.
The one action
  • Page background#fdf3ef
  • Panels and cards#f4e4dd
  • Borders and rules#e0ccc4
  • Secondary text#6d5950
  • Main text#26160f
  • Buttons and links#8f3b09
  • Highlights behind text#fedcce
  • 16.0 to 1 Main text on the page background needs 7
  • 6.0 to 1 Secondary text on the page background needs 4.5
  • 5.3 to 1 Secondary text on panels needs 4.5
  • 7.5 to 1 White text on a button needs 4.5
  • 6.9 to 1 Links on the page background needs 4.5
  • 13.6 to 1 Main text on a highlight needs 7

Paste this into your design spec

The accent is for things to act on and nothing else.

60, 30, 10

A rule borrowed from decorating a room. The largest share is calm, the next gives structure, and the smallest draws the eye. Judge it by eye: it is about weight, not a count of pixels. On a dense screen such as a dashboard the calm share is nearer 90.

60 background30 structure10

Easy. One sentence.
Made here with

Grow into

Use it for

One colour in even steps

Nine shades of one colour, from nearly white to nearly black, where each step looks the same size to the eye. Older colour sums make yellow steps look bigger than blue ones. The OKLCH way of writing colour fixes that, and current browsers understand it.

Hue 45

Hue 250, same steps

Ask for it like this

Make a nine-step scale of my brand colour from nearly white to nearly black, with even steps of lightness. Write the colours in OKLCH with a hex value beside each. Use the scale for backgrounds, borders and text of that colour.
Effort
Easy. One sentence.
Made here with
The CSS oklch() colour function
Grow into
A second scale for a neutral grey tinted with the same hue
Use it for
Design specs, charts in one colour, hover and pressed states

Colours that go together

Start from your colour and turn the wheel, keeping the lightness and strength the same. Because only the direction changes, the colours feel like a set. One of them is still the accent. The others are for charts, labels and pictures.

Neighbours

30 either side. Calm and close. Good for one mood.

Opposites

Half a turn away. The strongest contrast. Good for before against after.

Opposites, softened

Either side of the opposite. Lively without clashing.

Ask for it like this

Give me two more colours that go with my brand colour, for charts and labels: keep the same lightness and strength and change only the hue. Show neighbours, the opposite, and the softened opposite, and say which you would use.
Effort
Easy. One sentence.
Made here with
Turning the hue in OKLCH
Grow into
A palette for charts with up to eight series, checked for colour blindness
Use it for
Charts, labels, illustrations, a set of social pictures

Contrast you can read

Contrast is a ratio between the text and what is behind it, from 1 to 1 (invisible) up to 21 to 1 (black on white). Ordinary text needs 4.5. Two of these four pairs pass. The other two use colours that look fine side by side and still fail as text.

16.0 to 1. Passes.

7.5 to 1. Passes.

3.3 to 1. Fails for ordinary text.

1.4 to 1. Fails for ordinary text.

Ask for it like this

Check every pair of text colour and background on this page. List each pair with its contrast ratio, and fix any ordinary text under 4.5 to 1 or large text under 3 to 1 by changing the lightness, not the hue.
Effort
Easy. One sentence.
Made here with
The contrast sum from the accessibility guidelines
Grow into
A check for colour blindness as well
Use it for
Every page before it goes out

Your request

Build a proposal page from my notes in the practical instructor voice. The core idea in one sentence, one analogy, numbered steps with a time on each, and one next step. Look: my brand spec (attached). Make it one page that reads well on a phone, and mark anything you had to guess.

Recipe cards

A recipe is a page type: what goes on the page and in what order. Each recipe below has a finished example in the studio page (base/studio.html in the project, Recipes tab).

Choosing

If the page has to Use First-choice voice
Tell someone how a period went and what happens next One-page report Analyst
Get a customer to choose an option and say yes Proposal Practical instructor
Make a process or an idea understood Scrolling explainer Teacher
Get one kind of visitor to take one action Landing page Storyteller

If the content fits none of these, use the one-page report. It is the plainest and the hardest to get wrong.

One-page report

Field
Job Answer "how did it go, and what happens next" near the top
Sections, in order Title, period and reader. The whole period in two sentences. Four numbers, each with its change. One trend chart with a full-sentence heading. One breakdown table with the weak row marked. What changed. What happens next.
Parts Big numbers, line chart, table with a bar per row, two plain lists
Voices that fit Analyst, executive brief
Look Quiet. One data colour, grey for comparisons
Needs from the content The numbers for this period and the last, and the reader's name or role
Common mistakes A heading that names a topic instead of stating a finding. More than one chart per point. Totals that do not add up.

Proposal

Field
Job Turn a conversation into a decision
Sections, in order Cover: the promise, who it is for, valid until. What you asked for, in the customer's words. What we propose, with one drawing or image. Three options with the suggested one marked. Schedule. Included and not included. Terms. One button.
Parts Price cards, schedule chart, a drawing or photo, two lists
Voices that fit Practical instructor, executive brief
Look Calm, two colours, a serif for the large words
Needs from the content The estimate with line prices, the customer's own words, dates, terms
Common mistakes Prices that do not match the estimate. No "not included" list. More than one call to action.

Scrolling explainer

Field
Job Teach a process or an idea one step at a time
Sections, in order A title that names the process and one line on why it matters. A diagram or image that stays on screen. One block per stage: who does it, what happens, one fact. A closing line that adds the stages up.
Parts Pinned diagram or scrolling photo tour, a line that fills, small drawn icons
Voices that fit Teacher, practical instructor, keynote
Look Dark with one bright colour, or black and white with one highlight
Needs from the content The stages in order, who does each, and one fact per stage
Common mistakes More than seven stages. Blocks longer than three sentences. Motion that plays on its own.

Landing page

Field
Job Get one kind of visitor to take one action
Sections, in order The promise in one line with a number in it. One button. A picture of the result. What you get, as three things. How it works, in three steps. One customer's words. The price. Three real questions. The promise and the button again.
Parts Price cards, questions and answers, customer quote, one image or small animation
Voices that fit Storyteller, pitch, practical instructor
Look Two strong colours, and a third used only for the button
Needs from the content The offer, the price, the action, and real customer words if a quote is wanted
Common mistakes Two different buttons. An invented testimonial. Features listed where outcomes belong.

Adding a recipe

A new recipe earns a card when the same page type has been built by hand at least twice. Copy the table above, fill in every field, and add a finished example to the demo before listing it here.

Voice cards

A voice decides what is said, in what order, and how the page behaves. It is more than tone. The same facts told in two voices produce two different pages. Each voice has a full example in the studio demo (Voices tab), all seven making the same case with the same facts.

These are the canonical voice cards for this repository. Other tools that need a teaching or writing style should point here instead of keeping their own copy.

Each voice is inspired by a well-known communicator. That is a description of a style. Never write as if the person said it, and never put their name on a page.

Field
Inspired by Steve Jobs's product launches
Order The world as it is, as one painful number. The consequence. A question. The answer in three words. One image with the new number. Before and after. One more thing. A closing line short enough to repeat.
Sentences Very short. One idea each. Present tense.
Page behaviour One idea per screen. Screens snap into place. Words arrive in order.
Look Black background, one typeface, white and grey. Numbers enormous. One photograph, once, full screen.
Avoid Bullet lists, charts with axes, more than about twelve words on a screen

Storyteller

Field
Inspired by Donald Miller's story framework
Order A hook: one moment with a time and a place. A character who wants something. The problem at three depths: on the surface, underneath, why it is wrong. A guide with empathy, then proof. A plan in three steps. One call to action. The stakes: failure beside success. An ending that returns to the opening.
Sentences Concrete and visual. Past tense for the story, present for the offer.
Page behaviour One reading column. Photographs push in slowly. One pull quote per screen at most.
Look Colours taken from the photograph. Large serif type. Each story beat named in small type.
Avoid The company appearing before the fourth beat. An invented customer presented as real.

Teacher

Field
Inspired by David Malan's lectures
Order One question. An everyday analogy in very large type. One worked example with real values. The same idea as pseudocode or a diagram, stepped through. A harder case handled by what is already on the board. Questions to check understanding. A recap that reuses the analogy.
Sentences Plain, second person, one new term at a time
Page behaviour The reader does something: steps through, then answers
Look Black and white with one highlight that means "look here". Monospace for code. Every section tagged with what kind of thing it is.
Avoid Two new ideas in one step. An analogy that is dropped after the opening.

Pitch

Field
Inspired by Don Draper's carousel pitch in Mad Men
Order A personal memory in the first person. The feeling inside it. What was lost. One hard fact. What this is not, three times. What it is: the feeling, renamed as the product. A quiet close.
Sentences First person. Short. Never more than three under one image.
Page behaviour One slide at a time, advanced by hand
Look A dark room and one lit rectangle. Photographs faded and warm.
Avoid Feature lists, charts, the product name before the last slide. An invented memory: ask the person for a true one.

Practical instructor

Field
Inspired by A best guess at Bradley Ross's teaching style
Order The core idea in one sentence. One boxed analogy. Three numbers on why it matters. Numbered steps with a time on each. The same job at three levels. Common mistakes. One next step.
Sentences Start with a verb. No sentence that does not help someone act.
Page behaviour Everything the reader does is a control they can touch: tick boxes, a progress bar
Look A field guide or workbook. Two colours: one for structure, one that means "act". Tables for comparing levels.
Avoid Theory before the first step. Steps without a time estimate.

Analyst

Field
Inspired by Barbara Minto's pyramid principle
Order A title that is the conclusion. The answer in two sentences. Three numbers. Three findings, each with a full-sentence heading, one chart and a "so what". How it was measured. What it does not show. Next steps with owner and date.
Sentences Declarative. A number in most of them.
Page behaviour Charts can be touched to read values. Nothing else moves.
Look Quiet. One data colour, grey for comparison. Sources under each chart.
Avoid Headings that name a topic. Hiding the limits. Decoration that is not data.

Executive brief

Field
Inspired by The board or cabinet decision memo
Order Header: to, from, date, decision needed by. The decision. Background in numbered paragraphs. Options in one table, including "do nothing". Recommendation in two sentences. Risks, each with its control. Next steps.
Sentences Formal and complete. No adjectives that are not facts.
Page behaviour None. It is a document.
Look A paper page, one column, serif type, one accent colour for rules and headings
Avoid Images, animation, more than one page

Component catalogue

The parts a page can be built from. Each row is a working example in the studio. Pick parts that carry content; never add one for decoration.

Generated from the examples by _build/build.py.

Page components (no photo needed)

Component What it is for How it is made Grow into
Big numbers Three figures large enough to read from across a room. They count up once when they come into view. A few lines of script Motion or GSAP, for odometer-style digits
Timeline What happened, or what will happen, in order. The line fills as you scroll past it. A list and a CSS scroll-driven line GSAP ScrollTrigger, for stages that animate one by one
Process flow A small diagram that draws itself. It shows how a thing moves from start to finish. Hand-written SVG Mermaid for larger diagrams, GSAP for motion along the path
Comparison table Options side by side on the same questions, with the recommended one picked out. A plain HTML table shadcn/ui tables, for sorting and filtering
Price table Plans with one switch between monthly and yearly. The numbers change in place. Buttons and a few lines of script Magic UI or shadcn/ui pricing blocks
Questions and answers Each question opens on a tap. People read only the ones they came with. The HTML details element. No script. Nothing needed
Customer quote One person's words, set large. Use real words from a real customer, with their permission. Type and a background colour Nothing needed
Tabs Several short answers in the space of one. Good when readers want different things. Buttons and a few lines of script shadcn/ui tabs
Bar chart A handful of values compared. Thin bars, the number at the end of each, nothing else. Plain HTML and CSS Observable Plot or Chart.js, once you have more than a few bars
Progress ring One share of a whole. Use it for a single figure that matters more than the rest. Two SVG circles Nothing needed
Callouts A note, a warning and a confirmation. Each has an icon and a label as well as a colour, so it reads without the colour. CSS only Nothing needed
Old way, new way The change in two lists. The old one is struck through, so the eye lands on the new one. CSS only Nothing needed

Photo components

Component What it is for How it is made Grow into
Pan and zoom A still photo that moves slowly reads as film. Use it to open a page or to hold a quote. One CSS animation GSAP or Motion, for timed sequences of shots
Parallax window The photo moves slower than the page, so the frame feels like a window with depth behind it. CSS scroll-driven animation, plus a short script for older browsers GSAP ScrollTrigger, Lenis for smooth scrolling
Photo-filled type One word, large enough that the letters become windows. Good for a chapter break. CSS background-clip on text GSAP SplitText, to move each letter on its own
Scrolling photo tour The photo stays put while the text scrolls. Each paragraph moves the camera to the part it talks about. Sticky positioning and an IntersectionObserver Scrollama, the step-trigger library used in newsrooms
Self-drawing line art A sketch that draws itself as you scroll, then gives way to the real photo. The treeline, island and trunk were traced from the photo's own pixels. SVG paths and stroke-dashoffset, tied to scroll GSAP DrawSVG or Anime.js; Lottie or Rive for animation drawn by a designer
Chart from the photo A chart is a component too. These numbers are measured from the photo, so the chart and the picture tell the same story. Hand-written SVG, sized to your screen Observable Plot for quick charts, D3 for custom ones, ECharts for dashboards
Before and after Two versions of one picture with a divider to drag. It makes a change obvious without a word of explanation. A range slider, a CSS filter and clip-path Nothing needed. Supply two real photos in place of the filter.
Looks and voices The same photo and the same message, five ways. A look sets the mood; a voice sets how it speaks. Describe both and a page stops sounding generic. CSS filters, blend modes and the View Transitions API for the cross-fade A saved style card per look, so every page you make can reuse it
Frosted glass card Facts float over the photo on a pane that blurs what is behind it. The photo stays the star and the text stays readable. CSS backdrop-filter Magic UI or Aceternity UI, for ready-made animated cards
Bento grid A summary as a tray of tiles in different sizes. Each tile holds one fact, so the eye can land anywhere. CSS grid shadcn/ui and Magic UI, which ship bento layouts
Swipe gallery Cards in a row that snap into place one at a time. On a phone it is the most natural way to browse a set. CSS scroll snap. No script. Motion or GSAP, for dragging with momentum
Flip postcard A photo with a second side. Put the picture on the front and the message on the back. CSS 3D transforms and one line of script React Bits and Aceternity UI, which ship tilt and 3D cards

Pages

One-page report

A one-page report answers "how did it go and what happens next" before the reader has to scroll far. This one uses the analyst voice with a quiet look.

  • Short ask: Turn this spreadsheet into a one-page report: a two-sentence summary, four key numbers, one chart and what happens next.
  • Full ask: Build a one-page monthly report from my spreadsheet in the analyst voice. Title and period, a two-sentence summary, four key numbers each with its change from last month, one trend line with a full-sentence heading, one breakdown table with a small bar per row and the weakest row marked, then "what changed" and "what we will do next". One data colour, grey for comparisons.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Recipe: one-page report. Voice: analyst. Look: quiet, one data colour from my brand spec. Content: the attached spreadsheet and last month's report. Check that the breakdown rows add up to the totals and tell me if they do not.

Proposal

A proposal turns a conversation into a decision. It repeats what the customer asked for, shows the answer, prices it three ways and makes yes easy. This one uses the practical voice with a calm look.

  • Short ask: Turn my estimate and site notes into a one-page proposal with three price options and a schedule.
  • Full ask: Build a proposal page from my estimate and site notes. Cover with the promise, the customer and a valid-until date. Then "what you asked for" in their words, "what we propose" with a simple floor plan drawing, three options as price cards with our suggestion marked, a six-week schedule chart, included and not included, payment terms, and one accept button. Dark green and brass, a serif for headings.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Recipe: proposal. Voice: practical instructor. Look: my brand spec (attached). Content: the attached estimate, site notes and photos. Every price must come from the estimate; flag any line you could not match.

Scrolling explainer

A scrolling explainer teaches a process one stage at a time while a diagram keeps the reader's place. This one uses the teacher voice and no photographs at all.

  • Short ask: Explain my five-step process as a scrolling page with a diagram that stays on screen and lights up each step.
  • Full ask: Build a scrolling explainer of my process in the teacher voice. Title and one line on why it matters. Pin a diagram of the five stages at the top, with a small icon and label for each and a line that fills as I scroll. Under it, one block per stage: who does it, what happens in two or three sentences, and one fact set apart. End with a line that adds the stages up. Dark navy with one amber highlight.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Recipe: scrolling explainer. Voice: teacher. Look: dark with one highlight colour from my brand spec. Content: the attached procedure document. Keep my stage names exactly; if a stage has no fact worth setting apart, leave the fact out.

Landing page

A landing page has one job: get one kind of visitor to take one action. Everything on it either builds the case or removes a doubt. This one uses a plain confident voice and a moving ledger in place of a photograph.

  • Short ask: Make a landing page for my service with one clear promise, how it works in three steps, the price and one button.
  • Full ask: Build a landing page for my service. Open with the promise in one line that includes a number, and one button. Under it, show a short animated ledger with rows being ticked off. Then "what you get" as three numbered items, "how it works" in three steps, one customer quote, the price as two cards, three questions that open on tap, and the promise and button again. Deep teal, pale mint, and one coral colour used only for the button.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Recipe: landing page. Voice: storyteller. Look: take two colours from my logo (attached) and choose one button colour that appears nowhere else. Content: the attached service description and two customer emails. Use only real customer words for quotes; if I gave you none, leave the quote section out.

Voices

The keynote

The keynote voice sells a vision by removing everything else. Inspired by Steve Jobs's product launches. The company and every figure here are invented for the demo.

  • Short ask: Turn my notes into a keynote-style page: one idea per screen, huge type, almost no words.
  • Full ask: Build a keynote-style page from my notes. Black background, one sans-serif typeface. Open with the problem as one huge number, reveal the answer in three words, show my photo once full screen, compare before and after as two numbers, and finish with "one more thing". Screens snap as I scroll.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Recipe: scrolling explainer. Voice: keynote. Look: black and white, with one colour taken from my attached photo. Content: the attached notes. Mark any number you could not find in my notes instead of inventing one.

The storyteller

The storyteller voice makes the customer the hero and the company the guide. Inspired by Donald Miller's story framework. Priya, the company and the figures are invented for the demo.

  • Short ask: Tell this as a story on one page, with my customer as the hero and us as the guide. Use my photo large.
  • Full ask: Write a one-page story from my notes. Hero: my customer. Open on one moment with a time and a place. Give the problem at three depths, then introduce us as the guide with empathy before proof, a three-step plan, one button, the stakes side by side, and an ending that returns to the opening. Dark warm page, large serif type, my photo with a slow push-in. Take the colours from the photo.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Recipe: landing page. Voice: storyteller. Look: take the palette from my attached photo. Content: the attached customer interview notes. Invent nothing about the customer; where a story beat has no material, ask me one question.

The teacher

The teacher voice makes a hard idea feel obvious by starting somewhere familiar. Inspired by David Malan's lectures. The company and the timings are invented for the demo.

  • Short ask: Explain this like a great teacher: start with an everyday analogy, then one example, then the detail.
  • Full ask: Build a one-page lesson from my notes. Open with the question. Give one everyday analogy in very large type, then one worked example with real times, then the same idea as numbered pseudocode I can step through line by line, then three check-yourself questions that open on click, and a one-sentence recap that reuses the analogy. Black and white with a single highlight colour.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Recipe: scrolling explainer. Voice: teacher. Look: black and white with one highlight colour. Content: the attached procedure. Keep every step of my procedure; if the analogy stops fitting at some step, say so rather than bending the step.

The pitch

The pitch voice sells a feeling and lets the product arrive last. Inspired by Don Draper's carousel pitch in Mad Men. The father, the shop and the figures are invented for the demo.

  • Short ask: Pitch this as a feeling, not a feature. First person, a handful of slides, and the product named only at the end.
  • Full ask: Build a six-slide pitch from my notes that I advance by hand. Dark background with one lit slide at a time. Open with a personal memory in the first person, name the feeling, show what was lost, give one hard fact, say three things this is not, then name the product as the feeling. Make my photos look like faded film. End with a short close below the slides.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Recipe: landing page. Voice: pitch. Look: faded film, taken from my attached photos. Content: the attached notes. The memory must be mine: ask me for one true memory before you write, and do not invent one.

The practical instructor

The practical instructor voice gets someone doing the thing within the hour. A best guess at Bradley Ross's teaching style: core concept, one analogy, steps for today. The company and figures are invented for the demo.

  • Short ask: Turn this into a practical one-page guide: the core idea, one analogy, then steps I can do today.
  • Full ask: Build a one-page field guide from my notes. Start with the core idea in one sentence, then one boxed analogy, three numbers on why it matters, five numbered steps with a time estimate and a tick box each plus a progress bar, a table of the same job at beginner, advanced and expert level, three common mistakes, and one next step. Navy and one bright accent, condensed headings, squared grid paper background.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Recipe: scrolling explainer. Voice: practical instructor. Look: field guide in my brand colours (attached spec). Content: the attached procedure. Give every step a time estimate; ask me for any you cannot judge.

The analyst

The analyst voice gives the answer first and then earns it with evidence. Inspired by Barbara Minto's pyramid principle. The company and every figure are invented for the demo.

  • Short ask: Write this up as an evidence-first one-pager: the answer at the top, then three findings with a chart each.
  • Full ask: Build an evidence-first report from my data. The title states the conclusion. Then the answer in two sentences, three key numbers, and three findings where each heading is a full sentence with one chart and a "so what" line. Add how it was measured, what it does not show, and next steps with owner and date. One data colour, grey for comparisons, values labelled at the bar ends, source under every chart.

The executive brief

The executive brief voice exists to get a decision from busy people. It is the plainest voice here on purpose. It follows the convention of a board or cabinet decision memo. The company and figures are invented for the demo.

  • Short ask: Write this as a one-page decision brief for busy executives. Decision first, then background, options, recommendation and risks.
  • Full ask: Build a decision brief from my notes that looks like a paper memo. Header with to, from, date and decision deadline. State the decision first in a shaded box. Background in numbered paragraphs. One options table including "do nothing", with the recommended row shaded. Then the recommendation in two sentences, each risk with its control, and next steps. Serif type, one navy accent, no images, no animation.

Decks

Visionary deck

The visionary deck is for a room. It makes people feel that something has changed, and it leaves the detail for the conversation afterwards. It follows the manner of Steve Jobs's product launches: a villain, one rule, three things, one number, and a quiet last slide. The company and figures are invented.

  • Short ask: Turn my notes into a keynote-style deck: black slides, one idea each, huge type.
  • Full ask: Build an eight-slide deck from my notes in the keynote voice, black with white type. Slide 1 the feeling in one sentence, 2 the problem as one number, 3 what it cost, 4 the idea as one rule, 5 three things in three words, 6 the proof number with the old one struck through, 7 what it bought, 8 "one more thing" with the next step. No bullet lists. Make it one HTML file I can present with arrow keys.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Template: visionary deck. Content: the attached notes. Invent no facts and mark every gap.

Story deck

The story deck is for winning one customer or one room of them. The customer is the hero and the company is the guide. It follows Donald Miller's story framework: a character, a problem, a guide, a plan, a call to action, what failure looks like and what success looks like. The company and figures are invented.

  • Short ask: Turn my notes into a short story deck where my customer is the hero and we are the guide.
  • Full ask: Build a seven-slide deck from my notes in the storyteller voice, warm paper look with a serif headline. Slides: the person and what they want, the problem and how it feels, us as the guide with one proof, a three-step plan, one call to action, what happens if nothing changes, and what success looks like. Put a photo on the first and last slides only. Make it one HTML file I can present with arrow keys.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Template: story deck. Content: the attached notes and photo. Invent no facts and mark every gap.

Briefing deck

The briefing deck is for a room that has to decide. It gives the answer on the first slide, so the meeting can end early, and it says what is not known before anyone asks. The company and figures are invented.

  • Short ask: Turn my notes into a short briefing deck for a decision: the answer first.
  • Full ask: Build a six-slide deck from my notes in the executive brief voice, clean light look with one blue. Slides: the recommendation in one sentence, three reasons, two numbers with what they were before, the options on one table with the recommended one marked, what we do not know, and the decision with a date. Make it one HTML file I can present with arrow keys.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Template: briefing deck. Content: the attached notes. Invent no facts and mark every gap.

Workshop deck

The workshop deck is for teaching a room one skill. People practise before the session ends: a picture to hold the idea, the steps, one worked example, then their turn. The company and figures are invented.

  • Short ask: Turn my notes into a short workshop deck that teaches one skill, with an exercise.
  • Full ask: Build a seven-slide deck from my notes in the teacher voice, warm white look with one deep green and yellow labels. Slides: what people will be able to do, a comparison to hold the idea, three steps, one worked example, an exercise with a time limit on a slide of a different colour, a three-question check, and a card to keep. Make it one HTML file I can present with arrow keys.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Template: workshop deck. Content: the attached notes. Invent no facts and mark every gap.

Social formats and animated SVG

Animated SVG

Each file is plain SVG with its animation written in CSS inside the file. That means it plays as an image, inside a page, or pasted into a slide tool that accepts SVG. Colours come from four variables with built-in fallbacks, so a page can recolour a part by setting them.

  • Short ask: Add a small animated picture of a line going up next to my headline.
  • Full ask: Add the "line-draw" animated SVG from the artifact studio beside my headline, recoloured to my accent colour, with alt text that says what the trend is. Keep it under 160 pixels tall and make sure it is still readable with motion turned off.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Component: line-draw.svg, recoloured to my brand. Place it beside the headline.

Social formats

A post is read in about a second, on a phone, among other posts. So each format carries one idea in very large type, and the brand is a small line at the bottom. The sizes are the common ones. Platforms change their preferred sizes, so check the platform before a campaign.

  • Short ask: Make a square social post from this one sentence, in my colours.
  • Full ask: Make three social pictures from my notes: a square post with my main claim in seven words or fewer, a portrait post with my best number and a before-and-after bar, and a link preview with the page title. Use the colours in my attached spec, very large type, and my company name small at the bottom. Give me each as a PNG at full size.
  • With the skill: Use the artifact-studio skill. Templates: social square, portrait stat and link preview. Content: the attached notes. Invent no facts.

Photo components

Pan and zoom

A still photo that moves slowly reads as film. Use it to open a page or to hold a quote.
